item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts.
item.description:
The American journal of psychiatry
Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling. Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 with ICD-11 catatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 with ICD-11 catatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional). Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Neural connectomes of verbal fluency in post-stroke aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
Verbal fluency tasks are widely used to assess language abilities and executive functions in both clinical and research settings. In post-stroke patients, prior research has indicated a significant hodological contribution to the neural basis of verbal fluency; however, this has largely been examined using lesion-based measures, predefined tractography approaches, and traditional diffusion metrics. Quantitative anisotropy-based structural connectometry derived from correlational tractography was employed to determine the white matter circuits underlying semantic and phonemic fluency in 44 patients with post-stroke aphasia. Both task types were found to be linked to anterior frontal connections of left-hemisphere dorsal and ventral associative pathways, as well as domain-general projection pathways. However, visual inspection of the connectomes, supported by supplementary cross-control analyses, suggested differences in the relative emphasis and distribution of pathways, with phonemic fluency aligning more with the dorsal stream, while semantic fluency showed greater reliance on the ventral stream and a wider range of cortico-subcortical connections. The findings contribute to current understanding of the neural networks of verbal fluency in aphasia, with potential relevance for clinical practice and research.

item.title: Neural discrimination of emotional prosody in natural sentences in 2- to 3-month-old infants using OPM-MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
From birth, infants are sensitive to the emotional prosody of speech, yet it remains unclear when the developing brain discriminates emotions conveyed by natural spoken sentences. Here, we recorded brain activity with optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) in 15 infants aged 2-3 months while they listened to semantically neutral sentences spoken with happy or angry prosody. Natural sentences elicited robust auditory evoked responses, with prominent components at 88, 216, 380 and 1,356 ms after sentence onset and sources centred on bilateral superior and middle temporal cortex. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis revealed that distributed neural activity discriminated recordings spoken with happy from angry prosody 346-454 ms after the onset of the prosodically prominent word (the first word carrying a pitch peak), despite no difference in global field power between conditions. This discrimination was transient, emerged before the end of the sentence, and was carried primarily by phase-locked delta-band activity, followed by later differences in induced alpha power. Angry prosody also delayed the late auditory response by approximately 15 ms with no detectable changes in amplitude. Our findings show that cortical responses to happy and angry prosody in natural speech differ by 2-3 months of age, and demonstrate that OPM-MEG combined with time-resolved decoding can reveal the temporal, spatial and spectral organisation of early emotional-prosody processing.

item.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

item.title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

item.title: A domain-general basal ganglia mechanism for inhibitory control during language comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Whether controlled language processing involves domain-general or language-specific neural circuits is subject of controversial debate. We tested whether the inhibitory control of linguistic activity shares a common neural process with motor inhibition in twenty humans undergoing intra- and extracranial neural field potential recordings and deep-brain stimulation. Engaging motor and linguistic inhibition simultaneously resulted in a significant behavioral cost, suggesting a shared underlying neural process. Indeed, neural decoders trained during motor inhibition were able to decode linguistic inhibition and vice versa. Depth-electrode recordings from the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a key basal ganglia area for inhibitory control, showed increased β-band (13-30 Hz) activity during both linguistic and motor inhibition. Finally, disrupting the STN via deep-brain stimulation impaired behavioral and neural signatures of both linguistic and motor inhibition. Together, these findings show that the inhibitory control of language and movement share a domain-general mechanism implemented via the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia.

item.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

item.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

item.title: Hierarchical Uncertainty Transformation During Multimodal Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Human communication requires combining information from different modalities even when each source is incomplete or ambiguous. Yet how uncertainty is coordinated as distinct semantic representations interact and converge remains unclear. Here we propose a hierarchical uncertainty transformation framework and test it across four gesture–speech experiments combining behavioral measures, information-theoretic modelling, and electroencephalography. Rather than being uniformly reduced as information accumulates, uncertainty changed its computational form across three interdependent levels: uncertainty within modality-specific semantic representations, bidirectional but asymmetric changes during cross-modal interaction, and uncertainty associated with multisensory convergence. These computational distinctions were accompanied by differentiated but temporally overlapping neural associations. Modality-specific uncertainty was expressed relatively early, whereas cross-modal transformation and convergence were most prominently associated with activity in the N400 range. Critically, both the neural expression and statistical coupling of these computational quantities varied with the semantic information available from gesture and speech. Together, these findings show that multimodal comprehension involves a context-dependent reorganization of uncertainty across interacting representations, providing a computational framework for understanding how coherent meaning emerges from heterogeneous and uncertain information.

item.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

item.title: Domestic water mineral exposure increases affective disorders vulnerability by impairing brain structural resilience
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The neural mechanisms linking environmental mineral exposure to affective disorders remain poorly understood. Here, leveraging the large-scale UK Biobank cohort ( n = 389,984), we investigate the impact of domestic water mineral exposure on mental health. Beyond identifying population association of individual water mineral calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg) exposure, we developed a water mineral mixture exposure index (WMEx) to model mixture effect of Ca and Mg exposure on affective symptoms and disorders. We found that each unit increase in domestic water minerals exposure was associated with up to 0.24 standard deviation increase in elevated depressive symptoms (Ca: β = 0.24, P = 3.12 × 10 − 126 ; Mg: β = 0.07, P = 1.23×10 − 24 ; WMEx: β = 0.23, P = 1.55× 10 − 249 ), as well as an increased prospective risk of affective disorder incidence during 15.3 years follow-up (full model HR = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.40–1.96), which were all well replicated. Neuroimaging analyses uncovered the underlying neural substrates, revealing that mineral exposure was linked to impaired brain structural resilience, quantified by a novel brain structural resilience index (BSRI) representing the coupling between gray and white matter structures. Critically, causal mediation analyses demonstrated that the compromised brain structural resilience within visual-emotional circuits significantly mediated the pathway from mineral exposure to affective disorders. These neuromediating pathways were disproportionately stronger in females and individuals living in lower socioeconomic regions. Our findings reveal a crucial environmental-neurobiological axis, positioning domestic water minerals as a key determinant of mental health and highlighting how compromised brain structural resilience serves as a core neural mechanism of affective vulnerability.

item.title: Physiological Representation of Social Evaluation: Modeling Human Eye Movements, Pupillary, and Neuronal Responses to Faces.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Face-based social evaluations are ubiquitous and consequential, yet it remains unclear how these evaluations are represented in spontaneous physiological responses. Across four studies (222 participants: 142 females, 57 males, 23 unreported; 503 neurons), we used a data-driven modeling framework to examine how facial appearance shapes eye movements, pupillary responses, and neuronal activity during face viewing. We asked what these responses reveal about the underlying social evaluations. Pupillary responses and hippocampal firing during saccades were driven by facial variation associated with an integrated combination of valence and power evaluations; fixation duration on the eyes and hippocampal firing during fixations were more selectively tuned to threat-related evaluations; amygdalar firing primarily tracked approachability-related valence. A prospective validation study confirmed that novel faces synthesized along these modeled directions elicited the predicted physiological responses in new participants. We also found evidence of individual differences: social anxiety selectively heightened the sensitivity of pupillary responses to face evaluations. These findings suggest that distinct physiological responses across attention, autonomic arousal, and medial temporal lobe activity reflect distinct but related facets of face-based social evaluation.Significance Statement Everyday social decisions hinge on split-second impressions of unfamiliar faces. When we see a face, we instantly judge the person's likely intention (positive ↔ negative valence) and social influence (high ↔ low power). Across four complementary studies, we show that these evaluative processes are reflected in physiological responses to faces across overt attention, autonomic arousal, and subcortical neuronal firing. Different physiological systems reflected partially distinct but related facets of social-evaluative meaning, including integrated valence-and-power, threat-related, and approachability-related evaluation.

item.title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration.
item.description:
PLoS biology
The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

item.title: Limbic network hyperconnectivity, fasting appetite hormone dysregulation and impaired go/no-go performance in youths with bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BJPsych open
Background Bipolar disorder in youths is associated with metabolic dysregulation, impaired inhibitory control and limbic network connectivity changes. Aims To investigate whether limbic network connectivity is associated with appetite hormones and inhibitory control in youths with bipolar disorder. Method The current study included 68 youths with bipolar disorder and 57 age- and gender-matched controls. They completed clinical assessments, the go/no-go (GNG) task, fasting appetite hormone (leptin, adiponectin, insulin and ghrelin) tests and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI functional connectivity was analysed across 17 limbic ROIs. Cluster-level inferences were derived by using threshold-free cluster enhancement with family-wise error correction (p < 0.05). Furthermore, associations with appetite hormones and GNG task parameters were investigated. Results Compared with the control individuals, youths with bipolar disorder exhibited elevated leptin (p = 0.005) and insulin levels (p < 0.001), poorer performance on the GNG task and hyperconnectivity within the limbic network, identifying a significant cluster comprising the right anterior parahippocampal gyrus (aPHG)-right thalamus and right aPHG-hypothalamus edges (cluster-level family-wise error-corrected p = 0.045). No significant correlations were observed between limbic hyperconnectivity, appetite hormone levels and GNG task performance. Conclusions Current cross-sectional cohort indicates that youths with bipolar disorder exhibit concurrent alterations in appetite hormones, inhibitory control and limbic connectivity. These findings provide a characterisation of youth bipolar disorder across multiple indices, although longitudinal studies are necessary to understand how these features relate to long-term clinical trajectories.

item.title: Tractography-Based Insights into Neuroplasticity and Clinical Heterogeneity in Parkinson's Disease Subtypes.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Parkinson's disease shows substantial heterogeneity across motor, cognitive, and non-motor domains, reflecting variable patterns of neurodegeneration and compensation across distributed brain circuits. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography enables pathway-specific characterization of white-matter alterations and provides a framework for linking clinical subtypes to tract-level patterns that may be obscured by skeleton-based or connectomic averaging. Here, we synthesize white-matter evidence across motor, cognitive, genetic, and prodromal dimensions of PD heterogeneity, using tractography as an organizing framework within a broader dMRI and multimodal context. We review diffusion approaches ranging from diffusion tensor imaging to free-water, neurite, and fixel-based models. We distinguish pathway reconstructions from other diffusion and imaging analyses and consider how complementary approaches inform, but do not uniquely determine, interpretations of degeneration and subtype-specific neuroplasticity. Emerging methods, including harmonization pipelines, radiomic tractometry, and machine learning classifiers, may further improve tract-level sensitivity and reproducibility. Cognitive subtypes illustrate how posterior association and limbic tract degeneration, together with cholinergic and noradrenergic dysfunction, shape clinical progression. Integrating tractography with molecular, genetic, functional, and clinical markers may support subtype-specific biomarkers for risk stratification, prognosis, and targeted neuromodulation or rehabilitation strategies, although longitudinal and external validation is required before routine use.

item.title: Brain network functional connectivity alterations associated with acute posttraumatic headache.
item.description:
Headache
Objectives/background To investigate disruptions in resting state networks in participants with acute posttraumatic headache (PTH) due to mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated alterations in functional connectivity (FC) within core resting-state networks in participants with headache versus healthy controls (HCs), which may provide insights into disease mechanisms; however, the extent to which these alterations relate to PTH remains incompletely understood. Methods In this comparative cross-sectional study with an embedded prospective cohort, participants with acute PTH and HCs were enrolled from the Mayo Clinic Arizona and Minnesota, and the Phoenix Veterans Affairs Health Care between 2020 and 2024. Participants with PTH underwent resting-state magnetic resonance imaging within 2 months following mTBI. We investigated differences within and between functional brain networks in participants with PTH compared to HCs. Associations between altered FC with headache frequency, alterations of mood, post-mTBI symptoms, and concussion history were determined and corrected for age and sex. Relationships between PTH outcomes at 3 months and baseline FC were investigated. Results Ninety-six participants with acute PTH (35 male, 61 female) and 84 age-balanced HCs were included. Decreased resting state network connectivity in participants with PTH compared to HCs (False Discovery Rate (FDR) corrected <0.05) was observed in two default mode network (DMN) regions encompassing the bilateral frontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), as well as the left postcentral gyrus. Within those DMN regions, exploratory analyses revealed that FC was positively associated with headache frequency in the bilateral ACC, right precuneus and frontal gyrus, and with trait anxiety in the right ACC. In contrast, negative associations were observed between FC and number of mTBIs, as well as state anxiety, in the left ACC (uncorrected, p<0.05). No significant associations with clinical headache variables were observed in the DMN comprising the left postcentral gyrus. Baseline group differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were found in visual, sensorimotor, default mode, executive control and salience networks. Alterations in baseline connectivity between independent components in recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons. Conclusion In participants with PTH, the DMN regions showing decreased connectivity also exhibited associations with headache frequency, state and trait anxiety, and number of lifetime mTBIs, suggesting that these changes relate to the severity and persistence of post-mTBI symptoms. The baseline differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons, indicating that baseline network connections may not play a significant role in the recovery process.

item.title: Neural circuits, cognition, and behavior in diffuse glioma.
item.description:
Neuro-oncology
Diffuse gliomas arise within and become functionally integrated into neural circuits, establishing bidirectional interactions between malignant cells and the surrounding brain. Neuronal activity promotes glioma growth and progression, while glioma cells remodel the excitability, connectivity, and functional organization of the neural circuits they infiltrate. Pathological excitation-inhibition imbalance can impair cortical information processing, while tumor infiltration simultaneously disrupts, preserves, and induces adaptive reorganization of distributed functional networks. Language processing provides a well defined framework for examining these competing effects because language processing depends on distributed cortical and subcortical networks whose organization can be interrogated using neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and direct cortical stimulation. The pattern and severity of glioma-associated language dysfunction reflect the interaction among tumor location, growth kinetics, molecular and histopathological features, white matter involvement, and the capacity for adaptive redistribution of function within ipsilateral and contralateral networks. Slowly growing gliomas can permit substantial functional reorganization, whereas rapidly infiltrating tumors may constrain the time and biological substrate available for effective network adaptation. In this review, we examine reciprocal glioma-neural circuit interactions, with particular emphasis on the mechanisms of glioma-associated neuronal hyperexcitability and the disruption, preservation, and adaptive remodeling of language networks.

item.title: Reverberant magnetic resonance elastography and NODDI provide complementary characterisation of age-related brain changes in healthy adults.
item.description:
Physics in medicine and biology
Age-related changes in brain microstructure and mechanical properties are essential for understanding neurodegeneration and improving early diagnosis. We asked whether tissue microstructure explains the age-related decline in brain stiffness. To test this, we related stiffness measured using reverberant magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to tissue microstructure, assessed by neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI). Approach. Twenty-eight healthy volunteers (22 to 76 years) underwent 50 Hz MRE at 3T. NODDI parameters (the isotropic volume fraction, Fiso; orientation dispersion index, ODI; neurite density index, NDI) were computed from diffusion-weighted images in 26 subjects. We analyzed global gray and white matter, as well as 13 deep brain regions. Age associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations. Multivariate regression was used to test whether NODDI parameters predicted shear modulus independently of age. All tests used Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Main results. Shear modulus decreased with age in both gray matter (ρ= -0.62, p = 0.0005) and white matter (ρ= -0.60, p = 0.0007), and in nine of 13 deep brain regions after FDR correction. Fiso (ρ = +0.55, p = 0.004) and NDI (ρ= +0.45, p = 0.023) increased with age in gray matter; no NODDI parameter changed significantly with age in white matter. Across the six global multivariate tests (gray and white matter times three NODDI parameters), only the gray-matter Fiso independently predicted shear modulus after adjusting for age (β= -3.230, pFDR = 0.010), and no NODDI parameter predicted white matter stiffness. This association did not survive FDR correction after additional adjustment for sex (pFDR = 0.073). Significance. These findings suggest that cortical free water accumulation is the microstructural measure most closely associated with age-related softening in this cohort, pending confirmation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts, and support a multi-modal approach to characterizing age-related brain changes.

item.title: Abnormalities and plasticity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder: a BOLD fMRI study.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background This study investigated the architecture and neural activity of white matter functional networks (WMFNs) in individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD) after prolonged abstinence, compared with healthy controls (HCs). Methods Blood oxygen level-dependent signals in white matter were analyzed using a data-driven k-means clustering approach across individuals with OUD at baseline (OUD1), the same individuals after prolonged abstinence at follow-up (OUD2), and HCs. Results In OUD1, the deep frontoparietal network was fragmented into the superior longitudinal fasciculus network and anterior corona radiata network; this organization partially recovered in OUD2, becoming more similar to HCs. OUD1 also showed hyperactivation in the deep frontal network and hypoactivation in the frontotemporal-parietal network, with frontotemporal-parietal activity negatively correlated with years of opioid use. Conclusions OUD is associated with disrupted architecture of WMFNs and altered neural activity, whereas prolonged abstinence may promote partial network restoration. These findings highlight the neuroplastic potential of WMFNs during recovery and provide insights into the neural mechanisms underlying OUD and abstinence-related rehabilitation.

item.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural-behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility.
item.description:
Neuron
Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

item.title: Training Interbrain Synchrony through Dyadic Neurofeedback Modulates Empathy-for-Pain.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Dyadic neurofeedback offers a socially grounded approach for modulating neural processes that unfold between interacting individuals. While recent work demonstrates that dyadic neurofeedback can enhance inter-brain synchrony during interaction, whether its effects extend beyond the trained dyad remains unclear. Here, we examined whether dyadic neurofeedback targeting inter-brain synchrony in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is associated with changes in empathy-for-pain toward unfamiliar social targets. One hundred and eighty-six participants, randomly assigned to dyads, completed three neurofeedback training sessions within one week. Feedback was contingent on real-time IFG inter-brain synchrony in the neurofeedback group or on prerecorded signals in the sham-feedback control group. Empathy-for-pain was assessed before and after training. IFG inter-brain synchrony increased significantly across sessions in the neurofeedback group but not in the control group. Empathy-for-pain ratings showed different trajectories across conditions in the primary raw-data analysis, decreasing significantly in the sham-feedback group while remaining relatively stable in the neurofeedback group. A secondary analysis adjusting for a previously observed task-specific test-retest decline showed a significant increase in the neurofeedback group. Individuals with lower baseline trait empathy showed larger training-related increases in IFG inter-brain synchrony. Network analyses suggested broader changes involving IFG-IPL connectivity. Structural equation modeling further identified significant associations among training-related intra-brain synchrony, inter-brain synchrony, and empathy-for-pain change, consistent with the proposed relationship among these processes. Together, the findings indicate that dyadic neurofeedback can modulate IFG inter-brain synchrony across repeated training and may influence the trajectory of empathy-for-pain responding beyond the immediate training partner.

item.title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

item.title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

item.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

item.title: DPA: Deep Parcellation Analysis for Human Trait Prediction.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Mapping individual differences in white matter organization is a central goal of human brain mapping. Atlas-based structural connectome analyses are widely used but are sensitive to anatomical assumptions and may miss fine-grained connectivity patterns. Data-driven fiber clustering mitigates some limitations but typically relies on streamline endpoints, overlooking rich geometric information along full trajectories. In this paper, we introduce Deep Parcellation Analysis (DPA), a geometry-aware framework for white matter parcellation and trait association. DPA samples multiscale geometric features along entire fiber streamlines and encodes them with a Multiscale Fiber AutoEncoder (MFAE) to produce compact latent representations. These enable clustering that preserves intrinsic fiber geometry independently of anatomical atlases, supporting interpretable mapping of connectivity patterns linked to individual differences. Applied to diffusion magnetic resonance imaging data from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP-YA) cohort, DPA captures white matter substrates underlying language-related cognitive traits. It achieves comparable or superior predictive performance relative to atlas-based and principal parcellation approaches while revealing biologically plausible fiber pathways. Critically, DPA identifies trait-relevant connections missed by endpoint-based methods, emphasizing the importance of full streamline geometry. Overall, DPA demonstrates that deep, geometry-informed parcellation provides a powerful, interpretable approach for linking white matter organization to behavior, advancing structure-function studies in human brain mapping.

item.title: Directional Brain Connectivity Changes Induced by Heart Rate Variability Biofeedback: A Spectral Dynamic Causal Modeling Study.
item.description:
Applied psychophysiology and biofeedback
Heart rate variability biofeedback (HRVB) is a non-pharmacological intervention that trains individuals to breathe at their cardiovascular resonance frequency to enhance autonomic regulation. While HRVB improves cardiovascular function across clinical conditions, the directional neural pathways through which it modulates the central autonomic network (CAN) remain poorly understood. Using a publicly available open-access dataset, we conducted a secondary analysis of effective (directional) neural connectivity (EC) data from 32 healthy participants randomized to an 8-week HRVB intervention (n = 15) or a video game Control intervention (n = 17). Pre- and post-intervention resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were analyzed using spectral dynamic causal modeling (DCM) combined with parametric empirical Bayes to examine group differences in EC changes (ΔEC). We also evaluated whether connectivity changes correlated with changes in peripheral autonomic regulation, indexed by the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (ΔSDNN). Compared with the Control group, HRVB showed strong evidence (posterior-probability = 1) of increased ΔEC from the medial prefrontal cortex to the anterior cingulate cortex and bilateral thalamus post-treatment, along with reduced ΔEC from the right hippocampus to the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC). Furthermore, the regression coefficient linking hippocampus-to-VLPFC ΔEC with ΔSDNN was more (posterior-probability = 1) negative in the HRVB group than in Controls, indicating an intervention-dependent association between autonomic changes and effective connectivity. These findings indicate that HRVB may alter directional fronto-limbic communication within the CAN. Given the relatively small sample sizes, these findings need replication, but provide preliminary understanding about the neural circuitry through which resonance breathing may modulate central autonomic control.

item.title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

item.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross- and within-modal priming in Korean
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target’s written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O–P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350–550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250–350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O–P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

item.title: Brain Tissue Proportionality and General Cognitive Ability Across Three Adult Cohorts
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract General cognitive ability may relate to the proportional allocation of brain tissue beyond overall tissue volume. We examined five FreeSurfer compartments using compositional data analysis: cortical gray matter, cerebral white matter, subcortical gray matter, total cerebellum, and brainstem. Human Connectome Project Young Adult data (HCP-YA; N = 1,101) provided discovery estimates; the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study (DLBS; N = 418) and Amsterdam Open MRI Collection ID1000 (AOMIC; N = 926) provided independent cohort tests. Four isometric log-ratio coordinates represented composition, with age, sex, and log total analyzed tissue volume included separately. Composition explained additional cognitive variance in DLBS (partial R² = 4.20%, p = .00154) and AOMIC (partial R² = 1.35%, p = .014). The total-cerebellum-to-cerebral-white-matter contrast selected in HCP was positive in both replication cohorts: standardized β = 0.162 (heteroskedasticity-robust 95% confidence interval 0.072–0.252) in DLBS and 0.097 (0.024–0.170) in AOMIC. Participant-pairs bootstrap intervals supported both associations. Replacing total tissue volume with estimated intracranial volume attenuated the AOMIC association, whereas including both preserved it. Relative macroanatomical allocation is associated with broad cognitive ability conditional on analyzed tissue volume, with differing effect magnitudes across cohorts. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causal tissue trade-offs.

item.title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

item.title: Excessive censoring degrades individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized TMS targets.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Head motion systematically biases functional connectivity (FC) estimates in resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). A common mitigation strategy is to censor high-motion volumes and discard high-motion runs. However, overly stringent censoring risks discarding signal alongside noise, potentially degrading FC estimates. Here, we test the efficacy of various censoring strategies on individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) target selection. Using precision-fMRI datasets comprising 50 individuals, we define individualized "ground-truth" references from ≥1 hour of low-motion data per participant. We then simulate 10-minute or 20-minute rs-fMRI sessions with varying motion levels from the remaining data, yielding final samples of 22 and 19 participants, respectively. Higher motion produces parcellations and TMS targets that deviate further from the ground-truth references. However, at any given motion level, lenient censoring produces higher quality parcellations and personalized TMS targets than strict censoring. The improvement is comparable to doubling scan duration from 20 to 40 minutes under strict censoring. With personalized connectome-guided TMS, a common dilemma is whether to re-scan patients with only high-motion runs. A mixed-motion session with one low-motion run and one high-motion run may often be considered usable after discarding the high-motion run and strict censoring. We find that lenient censoring of high-motion-only sessions yields TMS targets comparable to-or even better than-those derived from strictly censored mixed-motion sessions. Therefore, within the motion range and parcellation/TMS targeting frameworks evaluated here, patients may not need to be re-scanned solely because all runs exceed strict censoring criteria.

item.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
item.description:
Journal of sleep research
Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

item.title: Animal fluency networks and item-based trajectories in people with Parkinson's disease before and after deep brain stimulation surgery.
item.description:
Journal of neuropsychology
Consistent decline in animal fluency occurs in people with Parkinson's disease (PD) post-surgery for Deep Brain Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS). Recent findings indicate that patients produce fewer words after (vs. before) surgery. Also, they produce smaller clusters of related animals, fewer switches between clusters, and more frequent (lexical frequency) and earlier-acquired words. In this paper, we further investigated difficulties in lexical retrieval by reporting on word networks (to study the structure of the mental lexicon) and item-based trajectories (to understand how the linguistic characteristics of the task change as the task progresses) of 61 Dutch-speaking individuals diagnosed with PD before and post-surgery for STN-DBS and 40 age and education-matched healthy controls. Word networks contained a higher number of edges and nodes for healthy controls relative to people with PD post-surgery (adjusting for differences in sample size). Also, patients before surgery produced a network with a lower cluster coefficient relative to healthy controls, as well as to people with PD post-surgery. Item-based trajectories showed that both healthy controls and people with PD produced words of increasing complexity as they proceed with the task (e.g., less frequent, acquired later, of higher length). Also, healthy controls showed a steeper increase in the age of acquisition of words across the first ten responses compared to PD post-surgery. The re-emergence of structure (clustering) in word networks post-surgery for STN-DBS and the differences in item-based trajectories (vs. healthy controls) represent novel markers of lexical retrieval that are affected by surgery for STN-DBS and PD.

item.title: Regional lesion burden and chronic post-stroke aphasia severity: Incremental value beyond total lesion volume.
item.description:
Applied neuropsychology. Adult
We examined whether regional lesion burden adds information beyond clinical variables and total lesion volume regarding chronic aphasia severity. This secondary analysis of the Aphasia Recovery Cohort included 195 participants with left-hemisphere stroke, Western Aphasia Battery Aphasia Quotient (AQ) ≤93.8, and assessment ≥180 days after stroke. Lesion burden was quantified in five atlas-defined groups. Partial Spearman correlations were adjusted for age at stroke, sex, time to assessment, and lesion volume, and four ridge-regression models were compared using 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation. A sensitivity analysis included participants whose imaging and Western Aphasia Battery assessments were ≤90 days apart (n = 128). Dorsal white-matter burden remained associated with lower AQ after adjustment (partial ρ = -0.261; false-discovery-rate q = 0.002). Adding regional burdens to the clinical-plus-volume model increased mean cross-validated R2 from 0.306 to 0.384 (ΔR2 = 0.078) and reduced mean absolute error from 18.76 to 17.31 AQ points. In the time-restricted sample, R2 increased from 0.312 to 0.442 (ΔR2 = 0.130), with the dorsal association persisting (partial ρ = -0.307). Regional lesion burden adds information beyond lesion volume and supports anatomical characterization of chronic aphasia severity.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)-a neural substrate of cognitive control-causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate-glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

item.title: Associations between nonfatal strangulation-related brain injury in intimate partner violence and resting-state functional connectivity.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Objective Examine the association between nonfatal strangulation-related probable brain injury (NFS-BI), resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and verbal memory, among females who experienced physical intimate partner violence (IPV). Method Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed for 110 females aged 18-60 years who experienced physical IPV. rsFC was characterized by seven graph theory metrics across three brain parcellation atlases (Power, Seitzman, and Schaefer-456 Parcellation[4S]). Responses to the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire determined IPV-head trauma frequency, experience of probable NFS-BI, and other/additional non-IPV and IPV-related BI. Verbal memory was characterized by three measures from the California Verbal Learning Test, Third Edition: (a) Long Delay, Free Recall, (b) Trials 1-5 correct index scores, and (c) memory retention from Trials 1-5 to Long Delay, Free Recall. Results NFS-BI was significantly associated with reductions in within-default mode network (DMN) connectivity (Power: B = -0.03, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -0.03, p = .005; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .03), DMN segregation (Power: B = -0.04, p = .006; Seitzman: B = -0.04, p = .007; 4S: B = -0.03, p = .02), and global modularity (Power: B = -0.01, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -0.02, p = .008; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .007). Interactions between NFS-BI and within-DMN strength (Power: B = -150.05, p = .03; Seitzman: B = -212.11 p = .01; 4S: B = -204.52, p = .002), DMN segregation (Power: B = -106.97, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -114.54 p = .008; 4S: B = -189.88, p < .001), and modularity (Power: B = -373.80, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -367.35, p = .001; 4S: B = -312.55, p = .006) were significantly associated with memory retention. Conclusions Those who experienced probable NFS-BI demonstrated altered rsFC compared with those who did not. Interactions between DMN rsFC and NFS-BI were significantly associated with memory retention. Future work should assess individuals with NFS-BI longitudinally to understand its effects on long-term brain health. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

item.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Non-invasive brain stimulation effects vary substantially across individuals, yet the physiological factors associated with this variability remain unclear. Objective We tested whether baseline and task-related EEG markers of excitation/inhibition (E/I) and hemodynamic state are associated with the effects of transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) on learning. Methods Participants completed a mathematical learning task during active or sham tRNS. We indexed E/I-related population dynamics using the EEG aperiodic exponent, for which lower values have been linked to relatively greater excitation than inhibition, and assessed hemodynamic state using fNIRS-derived oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO). Behavioral learning was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. Results tRNS accelerated learning relative to sham stimulation but did not reliably induce pre-post changes in resting-state aperiodic exponent or HbO. Instead, stimulation effects were state-dependent. Higher resting-state aperiodic exponent and lower resting-state HbO were associated with greater behavioral gains under tRNS, while task-related aperiodic exponent was associated with stimulation-related differences in learning. Task-evoked HbO was associated with learning rate but did not significantly differentiate stimulation effects. Across modalities, the findings identify complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic correlates of variability in learning under stimulation. However, statistical support for the EEG moderation effects was attenuated in models including participant-specific learning slopes, indicating sensitivity to random-effects specification and the need for replication. Conclusions The findings argue against a simple tonic-shift account of tRNS and support a state-dependent framework in which stimulation effects depend on ongoing electrophysiological and hemodynamic context. EEG and fNIRS provided complementary information about variability in learning and stimulation response, supporting multimodal approaches to understanding and individualizing neuromodulation.

item.title: Do autistic traits modulate the neural processing of logical rule violations in visual and auditory modalities?
item.description:
NeuroImage
Similarities in cognitive processing have been reported between individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and non-clinical individuals with autistic traits. However, previous research on autistic traits has primarily focused on social-emotional domains, with limited attention to abstract logical reasoning. Given that sensitivity to rules and patterns is a notable characteristic of the autism spectrum, logical rule processing may be particularly informative for understanding cognitive differences associated with autistic traits. The present research aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural responses of students with autistic traits to logical and illogical number sequences through two event-related potential studies. Based on Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) scores, participants were categorized into High-AQ and Low-AQ groups. In Study 1, both groups judged whether visually presented logical and illogical three number sequences followed a logical incremental rule. In Study 2, both groups performed the same task as in Study 1, except number sequences were presented in the auditory modality. No significant group difference was found in response to logical number sequences in either study. However, relative to the Low-AQ group, the High-AQ group exhibited larger P2 and P3 amplitudes and more negative emotional reactions to illogical number sequences in the visual modality (Study 1), and more positive N1 and LPP amplitudes, and higher arousal ratings to illogical number sequences in the auditory modality (Study 2). These findings suggest that students with autistic traits may exhibit altered neural responses and heightened emotional reactivity specifically to stimuli that violate logical rules in separate visual and auditory studies.

item.title: Same Networks, Different Dynamics: Parsimony in Auditory Cognitive Task Processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Distinct cognitive states might be supported either by dedicated, task-specific brain networks or by flexible modulation within shared ones, a distinction central to understanding how the brain allocates neural resources. Guided by the principle of parsimony, we hypothesized that both language and numerical cognition, when matched for sensory modality and attentional demand, would engage a common network architecture differentiated primarily through targeted modulation of connectivity strength and temporal dynamics rather than wholesale reconfiguration. We applied a jackknife-based dynamic functional connectivity approach to examine time-varying network engagement during auditory language comprehension and auditory math problem-solving in 172 age- and sex-matched participants from the Human Connectome Project-Young Adult cohort, using the Desikan-Killiany atlas and an 85% participation threshold. Of the significant connections identified, many were retained across both tasks, with 87 connections common to story and math, compared with 26 story-associated and 11 math-associated connections. Rather than indicating a novel shared-core architecture, this overlap is consistent with prior evidence that task functional connectivity is strongly constrained by a common intrinsic connectivity backbone. We therefore used the shared edge set as a common network framework for testing how two modality-matched, but cognitively distinct auditory tasks differ in connectivity strength and temporal variability. Among the 87 shared connections, 84 showed significant task-related differences in mean connectivity strength, indicating that story-math differentiation was expressed primarily through quantitative modulation of shared connections rather than wholesale changes in edge membership. Exploratory rolling-correlation analyses further suggested that some edges may show temporal variability in math-story connectivity correspondence even when mean connectivity strength is similar, highlighting a potential dynamic feature not captured by static connectivity estimates alone. Together, these findings suggest that story and math processing rely on a broadly shared connectivity backbone, while task differentiation emerges through graded modulation of connection strength and, in some cases, temporal variability.
